title: How Do Habits Form?
paragraphs: Much of our daily behaviour is driven not by deliberate choice but by habit. Making breakfast, checking a phone or following a familiar route to work often happens with little conscious thought, which frees the brain to concentrate on less predictable tasks.

Researchers frequently describe habits as a loop made up of a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue might be a particular time, location, emotion or preceding action; the routine is the behaviour; and the reward is the satisfying outcome that makes the brain more likely to repeat it.

With repetition, control of the behaviour gradually shifts towards brain systems that handle automatic actions. Once that happens, the cue can trigger the routine even when the original reward is no longer very attractive, which helps to explain why unwanted habits persist and why willpower alone is often not enough to break them.

Forming a new habit is usually slower than people expect. In a study at University College London, participants took an average of 66 days for a daily behaviour to feel automatic, with individual results ranging from a few weeks to many months. Practical strategies include starting with very small steps, attaching the new routine to an existing cue and changing the environment so that the desired behaviour is easier.
